group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature

explain.say: Most oil and gas began as tiny sea creatures and algae called plankton. When they died, they sank and were buried in mud on the sea floor with little oxygen.

explain.say: Over millions of years the mud was buried kilometres deep and became rock. Heat cooked the remains, slowly turning them into oil, and with more heat, into natural gas.

explain.say: Where a layer of tight rock, like shale or salt, sits on top, the oil and gas get trapped beneath it, gas at the top, then oil, then water. That trap is where we drill.

faq.a: No. Almost all oil comes from tiny sea plankton and algae buried in sea floor mud over millions of years. Dinosaurs are not a real source of oil.
asks: Did oil come from dead dinosaurs?

faq.a: Cap rock is a layer of rock, like shale or salt, that oil and gas cannot pass through. It acts like a lid and traps them underground.
Usually not. Oil sits in tiny spaces between grains of rock, like water in a sponge. Drilling lets it flow out of these pores.

faq.q: Why is gas on top of the oil?
faq.a: Natural gas is lighter than oil, and oil is lighter than water, so in a trap they separate into layers with gas at the top, oil in the middle and water below.
asks: Why do oil and water separate underground?

faq.q: How long does oil take to form?
faq.a: Millions of years, usually tens of millions. That is why oil is not renewable: we use it far faster than nature makes it.

facts: Most crude oil formed from marine plankton and algae buried in sea-floor sediments.
Oil forms at roughly 60 to 120 degrees Celsius; hotter conditions produce natural gas.

quiz.say: In an oil trap, what is usually found at the very top, just under the cap rock?
quiz.show: At the top of the trap:
quiz.why: Gas is the lightest fluid, so it rises above the oil, which rises above the water.

wrong.1: Oil sits below the gas because it is heavier.
wrong.2: Water is the heaviest, so it is at the bottom.
